The yanggeum is played by striking the metal strings with a thin bamboo stick with one hand. 
One set of string consists of four strings and totally fourteen sets (total 56 strings)are placed on two frets on a trapezoid sound box. It was imported and introduced in 18th century.
A type of Armenian folk cello

The beopgo, also called "honggo" is a drum used in Buddhist ritual. The size of it varies from a small one like the beokgu of farmer's music to a large one in 2 meter diameter. The beokgu is also called "beopgo."  The cowhide drum head covers the body made of well-dried wood. The drum body is put on a wood rack
Single-string spike fiddle with two holes in the soundtable from Zaghawa and Kanembu and other people in north-eastern and north-western Chad
Jua is peg of Haeguem

Small polish fiddle. Suka is known thanks to an item from the Biłgoraj area, Poland, shown at the First Polish Music Exhibition in Warsaw in 1888 (written accound by Jan Karłowicz, sketch by Tadeusz Dowgird, 1888, watercolour painting by Wojciech Gerson, 1896); in the second half of the 19th c., and possibly at the beginning of the 20th c. it was used in the south of the Lublin region (Biłgoraj area), probably accompanied by a single-skin drum; now used by artists of the folk revival; suka is played in the vertical position (hung over the shoulder on a string or leaned on the knee); players applied side string shortening (so-called fingernail technique)

The hun is a Korean ocarina-like flute  made of baked clay. 
It has a globular shape, with a blowing hole on top and five finger holes. The musicians play holding it with two hands, closing and opening the holes.
Flûte originaire du Laos et du Vietnam, similaire au bawu
Two-stringed fiddle of the Tuva people of Siberia, often with horse head on pegbox
Two-stringed tube fiddle from Guangxi and Ghuizhou provinces in China; the name means 'horse bone fiddle', the resonator is made of horse bone
Long-neck fretted fiddle from Bengal (India and Bangladesh). Soundboard pear-shaped and waisted
Hautbois cylindrique turc
Toje janggu is a kind of hourglass drum of which the body is made of clay.

The daegak is one of the trumpest used in the royal palace during the Joseon Dynasty. 
It is structured in several parts, including wide bell shape "daegu," thin pipe, and mouth piece. It is made of hammered silver, and colorful knots are attached to the wide bell part.

Small double-skin barrel drum of the Kongo-Vili and Kongo-Bembe peoples of the Kouilou and Bouenza regions in the lower Republic of the Congo. Both skins (goath or antilope) are laced together over the sound box with woven chords
Large double-headed cylindrical drum from the Nuni people of Burkina Faso
Rattle consisting of a woven vessel, attached to a stick, of the Fang in Gabon
Short-necked fiddle from Greece, with a pear-shaped body and two D-shaped soundholes in the soundboard; usually three strings

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: Viool met meetrillende snaren / viool d'amore

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) from the Marka people in Burkina Faso, and the Wolof people in Senegal and the Gambia

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: Tambor amb forma de rellotge de sorra
Tambor en forma de reloj de arena

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Lute from the Teke People in the Republic of Congo. Used to accompany ritual and popular dances
Stick zither with one resonator and 5 strings from the Lobi people in Burkina Faso
Small wooden sculpted flute with fingerholes, in the form of a stylised bird, from the Nuni people of Burkina Faso
Cylindrical friction drum of the Kongo people of the Bouenza region (Mouyondzi) in the Republic of Congo, Used to accompany religious and laic songs
Kettle drum from the Gouin eople in Burkina Faso played with two wooden sticks
Gulmancé term for the Griot lute in Burkina Faso
Two-string fiddle of the Han Chinese, especially from the north; smaller than erhu
Single-string fiddle of Yugoslavia, often with horse-head decoration on top of neck
Large conical drum from the Gan people in Burkina Faso

Double-headed tuned cylindrical drum of the Mijikenda-Digo  people of the coastal region of Kenya. Forms a family with the mchirima set of drums. The separate drum gives the rhythm while the four others give some sort of a song. The chapuo is played on both sides. Tuning by tightening the chords by hitting the rings on which the membbranes ore stretched; held horizontally, tied to the waste; 2 pitches, each membrane is tuned differently. The whole set is used in the Sengenya dance, and used to heal sick persons; it takes a whole night to heal
The sogo is a small drum covered with linnen and animal skin. Just like the daego it is painted in red and with peony and then covered with skin.

The wonsan, made of a piece of gourd, is a bridge which support the two strings. 
It is put on the center of one side of the soundbox, but it is moveable to control the volume. Wonsan is put in the center to make louder volume, but the volume becomes weaker when it is moved upside.

The noego is a drum set with six small drums colored in black. Each drum has only one drum head. The cone shaped side of the drums are put together and hung horizontally in a wooden frame. It was used in sacrificial rites for heavenly gods

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: Bęben klepsydrowy ze zmiennym napięciem membran

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Single or double woven rattle with handle from the Kongo and Bembe people of the Bouenza region in the south of Republic of the Congo

The eunggo is a drum hung on a wood frame decorated with phoenix and the moon on top. It was used for music of royal event and court banquet, put in the east side of the orchestra. When starting the music, sakgo, eunggo, and the geongo are hit in order as a set
The ajaeng is a bowed zither with seven strings. Its lower body is also bent like the daejaeng, but the ajaeng is smaller and uses a bow.
Double-headed ylindrical drum of the Yana and Moosè people in Burkina Faso. 'Gangango' means 'drum' in Moorè language. The generic name in West and North African cultures is 'Ganga'

"The jing is brass gong and is played with a stick covered with soft cloth. 
According to the treatise of Akhakgwebeom (1493), it is described that the stick is covered with deer skin." (Gugak center, Korea)

Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum), from the Siamou people in Burkina Faso (compared to the other Burkina talking drums there are considerably fewer strings attached to change the tensions of the membranes)

Spike fiddle of the Batak Karo and Batak Toba areas in North Sumatra, Indonesia. Its spike and neck are made of wood and its gourdshaped body of coconut shell, 8 to 15 cm in diameter. The top of the neck may be decorated with a carved scroll. Two strings

The taepyeongso is a wind instrument hold like the trumphet. It has eight finger holes on a conical wooden body with a metal mouthpiece and a cup-shaped metal bell, called dongpallang. It is mostly arranged in military-related music.
Two-stringed spike tube fiddle of Thailand, resembling the Chinese erhu
Bell of the Teke people in the Cuvette and Plateaux region of Republic of the Congo. Made of buffle horns
Double terra cotta kettledrum from the Siamou people in Burkina Faso

The yak is a vertical wind instrument which used to be arranged in court ritual and ceremonial music. It is made of bamboo with three finger holes. Not as a music instrument, but as a dance prop, a smaller size yak is also used in court ritual civil dance. The dancers hold yak in their left hand.
Rattles made of  small dried fruits strung to a strap, from the Mbosi-Makwa people in the Cuvette region of Republic of the Congo
The yo is one of the four metal instruments that are tak, sun, and tak. Even though it is classified as one of the aak musical instruments, it plays role more as a ritual object

Shaken rattle of the Mijikenda people of the coastal areas of Kenya. Bottle tops in an open woven basket-like container are shaken and struck; the bottle tops slide on the basket. The basket has a handle to hang it on the wall or to transport it. The bottle tops are then put in a separate container. The Uteo can play the beat when shaken and can also imitate the movement of the women who separate the dirt from the millet or beans or grains
Balafo with 14 lamels arranged on a strongly curved base from the Bwa people in Burkina faso
The junggo is similar to the gyobanggo, but a bit larger and longer. It was used when dancing for dukje ritual.
Double-headed cylindrical drum from the Winnè people in Burkina Faso

Two-stringed spike fiddle from Korea with wooden soundboard.
"The haegeum is two string fiddle with a bow. The instrument is structured in a soundbox and a lodlike neck. Left hand hold and grasp the strings to make pitch and the right hand controls the bow across."

The beokgu, also called "sogo," is the smallest drum used in the farmer's music. The skin of the two small drum heads are connected with the rope on the body. A finger-thick wood stick of a handspan long is used to hit the center of the heads or the body.

Vessel rattle made from a big dried longitudinal bean-like fruit, from the Teke-Kukuya people in the Plateaux region of Republic of the Congo. Called Oumouaka by the Pygmee people of Republic of the Congo
Flûte oblique d'Arménie, d'origine pastorale et semblable au blur turc
Ox horn fiddle from the Buyi people in southern China, the resonator being of ox horn and the neck of wood
Vessel rattle (hollow stick) of the Fang in Gabon

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: 高压气体使弦发音的钢琴

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Janggu chae is the thin cane like bamboo stick used to hit the right drum head of the janggu

Adeudeu. Arched harp of the Teso people of Uganda and Kenya"
Music Dept, Kenyatta Univ: "The adeudeu is often played by two players, one plays the strings, the second player plays the rhythm with a  hammer padded with cloath. The adeudeu plays the low ranges; accompanies songs; the singer also plays the harp. Solo performance  or played in sets of three. For entertainment. Normally played by men, not seldom elderly men who play it for mockery songs. Held in the arms with the soundbox towards the player. Played with the thumb and the index.
G. Senoga-Zake, Folk Music of Kenya, 2000, 140: "A five string type of harp used by the Iteso who live on the border of Kenya and Uganda in Busia District, Western Province, and whose cousins are found immediately on the other side of the border, in Uganda.
Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) from Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast
The wolgeum is a lute with four strings. It has a moon shape body with a long neck on which thirteen frets are put. The tuning and playing technique are same as that of the dangbipa.
Iron double bell, often with a raphia woven handle from the Teke peoples in the Plateaux region of Republic of the Congo

The gwangsoe is a brass gong used in Buddhist and shaman music which is the middle size of a Jing and a Kkweanggwari.  It has a handle shaped like the Korean alphabet 'ㄱ', and It is played with a stick shaped like Kkweanggwari stick.

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: 罕用语](旧时舞蹈教师用的)小提琴

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Bow lute of the Teke people in Central Africa, the Congo's and Gabon. Five fibre strings are mounted almost perpendicular to a large sound box, on which geometrical decorations are engraved and burned. A buzzing effect is produced by metal jingles on the string-bearers
Hautbois de Catalogne
Cornemuse de Galice
Small side-blown wooden horn of the Moosé and Nuni people, Burkina. The mouthpiece is cut in the outer curve of the horn
Single-string fiddle (of the Songhay people?) of Mali; noteable performer Ali Farka Touré
The daego is a drum covered with colored linen and animal skin. Its wooden body, wrapped with linen, is painted in red and with peony and then covered with skin.

The noedo, colored in black, is a set of three small drums pierced crosswise on a long pole arranged with noego. When twisted the pole with both hands to play, the fine leather straps hit the six drumheads and make sounds
Wooden sculptured flute, closed at the end and with fingerholes. From the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
Small wooden sculpted flute (12 to 15 cm) with fingerholes, in the form of a stylised bird, from the Nuni people of Burkina Faso

A one-string musical bow with a resonator made of an inflated bladder. A traditional instrument. whose diffusion in the area of Northern Italy is attested by oral and written memory. The name denotes the instrument as well as the performer, often an itinerant
street player. The historical sources concerning the torototela indicate that this
instrument and musician already disappeared in the 19th century. Contrary to
this, oral records proved the permanence of the instrument until recent time,
in the Riva and Asti areas.
Two-string Chinese fiddle; a 'middle' erhu with an alto range

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: Piano in forma di tavolo da cucito

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Hautbois du Cambodge
Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) from the Gulmancé people in Burkina Faso
Large cylindrical footed drum from the Koyo and Banguele of the Cuvette region (Makoua) in the Republic of Congo. Used fot popular festivitie

The jingo is the largest drum among the drums placed on the wooden frame. The drum colored in red has two drum heads and put on the frame with four legs. The musician hits it with a stick covered with soft cloth one end

Triangual frame zither from the Lobi people of Burkina Faso, with several gourds attached as resonator, including one at the point of V of the arm. Six to nine strings. May have a metal buzzer at the end of the arm
Cornemuse du Val d'Aran, sans bourdon et à anche simple
The sanjo ajaeng does not have its own bow manufactured but simply uses the cello bow.

Transverse flute of the Mijikenda-Rabai and -Digo people of the coastal region of Kenya; made of a bamboo stem of which a nod stops the end of the flute. Six fingerholes, one hole for blowing. The tube is decorated with burnt small crosses all over the flute. 
The chivoti plays melodic accompaniments. It accompanies songs and the sengenya dance.
Wooden griot lute from the Fulbé people of Burkina Faso
Large bowl lyre of the Gusii people in Kenya, with large flat bridge

A polish bagpipe with low tuning and elegiac sound; formerly used during the ritual part of the wedding ceremony together with mazanki, after World War II reactivated in the S. Moniuszko Music School in Zbąszyń and in the folk revival

The ji is transverse bamboo flute with five finger holes like the sogeum. 
There are four holes in the front and one at the back. The U-shape mouth hole is made separately and then attached to the pipe. The end of the pipe is carved in cross shape hole.
Movable bridge
Spike tube fiddle from Tibet/Bhutan, with a resonator made of wood, metal or ivory; it has two to four strings

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: Effetto sonoro degli zoccoli di cavallo

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Set of three drums (sing. = Engoma) of the Luhya-Bukusu people of West Kenya: usually one big drum and two smaller ones. They are held around the waist, with a belt. Played with two sticks, or with one stick and one hand. They are made of metal tanks, covered with cow hide on both sides, laced together with cow hide laces. They are smaller than the endumba drum, which fills in the base beats. The cing'oma  accompany the litungu and the ishiriri. Played in a set of three, but can also be played solo, in pair or in a set of more than three, according to the skills of the player. Played in the Kamobeka dance, completed with the Endumba / Indumba drum.
Large wooden drum with five big pegs, held in a vertical playing position. From the Bobo people in Burkina Faso

Dance rattle of the Meru people of East Kenya, provides percussive to the dance. It is held and shaken in one hand and hit with a stick with the other hand, causing a double percussive result: jingles and strikes of the stick to the wooden plate. Each dancer has one of this.
North African term for an oblique rim-blown flute

Three-string fiddle of Madhya Pradesh in India with a wooden soundbox; however, the kikirs in the FF database in M+ all have one string and a soundbox made from ceramic material (see description TUA-326); on the internet (see sources), the kingri is also said to have a resonator box made from unglazed pottery (New Grove)
Small end-blown wooden flute (15 to 20 cm) from the Bissa people in Burkina Faso
Vessel rattle of the Mobsi-Makwa people of Republic of the Congo. Made of a small calebash, of which the neck is closed with a cork
The banghyang consists of sixteen metal plates hung in a wooden frame with two parrall bars. Each bar has eight plates. It is hit with the stick made of cow horn. (Gugak Center, Korea)
Small wooden sculptured flute, often in the form of a stylized bird, with fingerholes, and open at the end. From the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
Three-stringed spike fiddle of Okinawa, Japan. The resonator is half a coconut shell, covered with snake skin

The saenghwang is a mouth organ with several bamboo pipes mounted vertically in a windchest made of dried gourd. 
Small metal boards resonate and make sounds as the musician blows in the air to the mouth piece or inhales. Saenghwang is the comprehensive term refferring to this type of instrument, and the instrument has different names based on the number of bamboo pipes put in the windchest.

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: 黑克尔管（上低音双簧管）

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Spike fiddle from the Arab world; may refer to both the spike bowl fiddle and the quadrangular spike fiddle
Fulbé term for the double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) in Burkina Faso
Vessel rattle made from a big dried longitudinal bean-like fruit, from the Teke-Nangoulou people in the Plateaux region of Republic of the Congo
One-stringed tube fiddle from Nyanja people in Mozambique; string is tuned with tuning loop around neck
Orgue à bouche du peuple Hmong
Single-string spike fiddle of the Susu people in Guinea and Sierra Leone
Side blown antelope horn of the Mbosi and Kongo people of the Congo's
Ji is the wooden pestle used to pound and to make sounds of the chuk

The sang is one of aak musical instruments but it plays role more as a ritual object. 
The ritual assistance puts it to the left side of the military dancers, and strike it to control the dancer's steps. The assistance holds the strap with the left hand and strike the drumhead with the stick in the right hand
Ancient Chinese lute. NB: in Metropolitan Museum this is described as a fiddle as it comes with a bow!

Small single-headed square frame drum from the Teke people in the Republic of the Congo. The skin is nailed to a robust wooden frame. Held between the legs, the pitch can be changed by the pressure of the heel on the skin. Used to accompany the danse 'okilidzéké' of the young people. Also used in the 1920's in the maringa, an urban music style attributed amonst other to the Loango region on the French Congolese coast, and described as 'Europeanized'  since it included also accordion and rhythms borrowed from polkas, marches, hymns, etc. The patenge is also played to accompany the rumba
'Flute of the conqueror'; end blown sculptured  flute from the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
One-stringed tube fiddle of the Chewa people in southern and central Malawi; the projecting tip of the neck acts as string-holder; Werner notes the term chimwenyuwenyu on Likoma island in Lake Malawi
Strung rattles made of folded palmleaves

Percussion instrument of the Kikuyu people of Central Kenya. Cog wheel; spare part for a car. Used to keep the tempo and to add tone colour. Previously made by blacksmiths. The player holds the instrument in the left hand and a beater, a steel rod, in the right hand. The sound is produced by hitting up and down the inside of the ring, which is usually brought to rest on a hard surface, such as a box, on the last beat of each bar. It is nowadays used to accompany the accordion especially the mwomboko dance

Compact large single-headed cylindrical drum with feet carved out of the base, and which is beated with a stick. Played by of the Mbosi-Koyo people in the Cuvette region of Republic of the Congo. Geometrical engravings decorate the body. Used in the Odaki (OdaKé) lovers dance, and in the Ekongo warriors dance
One-stringed fiddle of West African origin, used in Cape Verde
General term for fiddle in Central and Eastern Africa

Long cylindrical drum of the Chika and Embu-Mbeere people of Central Kenya. Carved from a large log. Held with a strap on the shoulder during playing, or taken between the legs, so that the players can dance. They change positions duirng the same dance. The drums are accompanied by a whistle, which controls the drum beats, and give the rhythm for the dance passes. It is played by men for entertainment; accompanment of the Mwinjiru dance
Long-necked fretted fiddle from North India and Pakistan; resonator like that of a sarangi (as opposed to the esraj)
Hautbois sri lankais
Single-string fiddle of the Pulluvan in Kerala, south India. The neck is glued to the soundbox and starts like a crescent which continues into a neck and ends in the pegbox

Percussion instrument of the Luo people of West Kenya. Two open metal rings which vary in pitches when struck.One is held by the big toe and the other one is held by the thumb. They are both placed on a wooden soundbox, of which the lower part is half open, and which is struck on the side as well with a rubber stick. The nyangile provides rhythm in the Ramogi dance and the Ohangla dance; in Ramogi it plays solo; in Ohangla it is played with the metal Ohangla drums.
Small wooden double bell of the Tsogho in Gabon
Kalapapla is a woman's drum .. Covered on one side and is made from a hollowed log. It is usually played in a group of three or more, at a funeral or parties.
Single-string spike fiddle of the Hausa in Nigeria, smaller than goge
Newly developed spike fiddle, created by Peter Biffin; there are several types; the instrument resembles a kamanche
Small fiddle from the Tatra mountains in Poland
Musical bow from the Samo peopàle in Burkina Faso consisting of a string supported by a flexible wooden string bearer.  A calebash is attached as resonator
Three-stringed spike fiddle of Thailand, resembling the Javanese rebab; resonator is coconut shell with three bulges on the back, covered with skin
Fiddle used by the Sundanese and Badui people in West Java, with a trapezoidal resonator. Often has a carved-out pegbox
The okdanso is a kind of danso which is made of jade. There are five finger holes and one hole is at the back.
The kkweanggwari is brass gong in small size. It is played with a wooden stick.
Rudimentary xylophone of the Bomitaba people of the Likouala region in Republic of the Congo. Played on the ground, with 5 lamellae

The ssangpiri, a wind instrument with reed, uses two bamboo bodies. Two pipes made of sinudae bamboo are tied together with silk or thin copper wire. There are six holes and one in the back and the other in the front. It is transmitted in Ganghwa region in Gyeonggi-do Province
Peul term for the one-stringed spike fiddle in Western Africa; note the soundhole in the soundbox, not in the soundboard
Wolof term for the single-string fiddle with gourd resonator from Senegambia; soundhole in soundbox, not in soundboard

The junggeum is a transverse wind instrument made of bamboo shorter than the daegeum. 
Along with the daegeum, it is one of the three bamboo flutes of the Unified Silla Period. According to Akhakgwebeom it is said to be the same as the structure of daegeum, but the junggeum has no membrane hole. It only has one mouth hole and six finger holes.
Instrument with free reeds (sort of harmonium) invented by Christian Dietz around 1830
The jwago is a drum hung on the wooden frame, and the musician always plays it sitting on the floor. The drumheads hung on square frame face left and right side
Conical drum of the Teke-Kukuya people of the republic of Congo

Seven-string bowl lytreyre of the Luhya-Bukusu people of West Kenya. Nowadays wooden (plywood) sound board instead of (lizard) skin. The sound box is made of carved out piece of wood. Nylon strings (they used to be made of tendons). Movable bridge for transposition. The tuning depends on the vocal range of the singer. Tuned by tightening the string on the wooden crosspiece. Tuning knobs made of old cloaths; they used to be made of dried banana leaves. One oval sound hole showing one of the arms; small square hole for decoration. The litungu lyre provides melodic accompaniment to dances. The player is usually a soloist; he plays and sings at the same time. He is often accompanied by the ishiriri/silili fiddle and /or the eshimuka shaker. Occasions: entertainment, harvest, competitions, beer drinking parties, child birth, story telling times

The yonggo is a barrel drum colorfully painted with dragons, and used in ""Daechwita"" music. "Daewhita" is a marching band music played for king's procession or military parade. It is similar to the gyobanggo but smaller. The metal tacks are embedded around the rim of both drum heads and the musician hangs it around his neck with the rope and thus strikes the drum from up to downward.

Gwea, the frets, are little piece of wood attached to the body and supports strings. 
The gwea is different from anjok, the moveable bridges, in its usage. Its size and shape are different depending on the instrument types, but most of the times, they are rectangular wood piece. They are attached on the soundbox and below the strings. The geomungo, hyangbipa, dangbipa, wolgeum, and yanggeum have the frets which enable the musicians push and pull the strings.
Hautbois cylindrique de la province de Sind (Pakistan)
The nagak, also called "sora" as it is a large seashell played as a horn. It is made by making a mouth hole at the end of a big seashell.

The tungso is a vertical wind instrument. 
Similar to the daegeum it has a membrane hole, but it has five finger holes in the front and one at the back. Like the jeok, it has extra holes at the bottom.

Set of four or five double-headed cylindrical drums of the Mijikenda people of the coastal region of Kenya. They are hung in a wooden stand.  The heads are fixed by secruing rings and lacing. The set is played with the chapuo. Al are tuned and are played as part of an ensemble that includes the chivoti and the kayamba. One person plays the four drums in a row, another drummer plays the chapuo separately. The chapuo gives the rhtyhm while the others give some sort of song. The set is used in the Sengenya dance. Collective of different rhythms; "they are gossiping together"
Small wooden sculptured flute, often in the form of a stylized bird, with fingerholes, and open at the end. From the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
[tro] Generic term for fiddles in Cambodja
Term for a North-African bamboo duct flute
Rattle consisting of a round woven vessel attached on a long stick. Of the Mbamba in Gabon
Urdu name for the long-necked fretted peacock fiddle in India and Pakistan; in northern India it is known as mayuri
Vietnamese two-string fiddle, resonator made of coconut shell

The so has sixteen bamboo pipes horizontally put in line in a phoenix shape wood body. The end of the pipes are closed with beeswax to control the pitch. The musician holds wood frame at both ends and blows air into the pipes.
The nabal is a long metal trumpet with a conical body. There is no finger hole
Single-string spike fiddle of the Bissa in Burkina Faso
Bullroarer of the Fang, Gabon
Two- or three-stringed spike fiddle of Georgia
The dangpiri is a double reed wind instrument which is hold vertically. There are eight finger holes on the bamboo body, and the second hole is at the back.
Mâchoire racle
Two-stringed calabash lute from the Bissa people in Burkina Faso
Spike fiddle of Iran with a spherical body often inlaid with mother-of-pearl or bone; formerly three strings, modern instruments have four
Side blown horn of the Kongo and Bembe people of the Bouenza region in the south of Republic of the Congo. Made from an antelope horn. 'Mvouri' = 'antelope'. Used to accompany songs calling for rain
Lamellophone played by Bwa, Ngbele, Mbuja, Budeu and Makere peoples

The yeonggo is a drum set with eight small drums colored in yellow. Each drum has only one drum head. The cone shaped side of the drums are put together and hung horizontally in a wooden frame. It was used in sacrificial rites for earth gods
Vessel rattle made from a big dried longitudinal bean-like fruit, from the Teke people in the Republic of Congo. Called Otsara by the Pygmee people of Republic of the Congo
Long elongated hourglass drum of about 100 cm from the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
Three-stringed box fiddle of the Inuit people

"The ulla is a percussion instrument comprising a set of ten small copper gongs in plate shape. There are two kinds of ulla with a wooden frame or a hand grip. When playing it walking and moving, musician holds the ulla with the grip in his left hand. When playing it in a appointed position, the musician uses the one on a frame." (Gugak Center, Korea)
Obsolete tuned metal gongs of Korea, the Korean name for Chinese Yunluo. The set of ten thin disc-shaped gongs were mounted in a portable wooden frame in three rows of three with a single gong on top ... The instrument is considered Chinese ... The only extant examples now in Korea, were brought from Beijing in 1937" (Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments, 1984)

One- or two-stringed archaic spike fiddle of the Iban of Sarawak, Borneo. Its soundbox is half a gourd or coconut shell, covered with animal skin. It exists in a simple form, without any decoration, and in a more elaborate form, where the top of the neck expands into a large disc carved into a floral pattern. The performer places the body of the instrument between his toes while sitting down, the knees bent outward and the soles of the feet together. The strings are moistened to produce the proper sound. The convex bow made of wood or bamboo is held in the right hand. There are specimens in the Museum Volkenkunde in Leiden, the Metropolitan Museum in New York, the Musée des Instruments de Musique in Brussels, the Sarawak Museum in Kuching and the Musée d'ethnographie de Neuchâtel
One-string fiddle with tin can resonator at the top end of the Tswana and Xhoisan people from Botswana
Corn stalk fiddle of Bosnia and Serbia

The yeongdo, colored in yellow, is a set of four small drums pierced crosswise on a long pole. It is arranged with yeonggo, and there are also eight drum heads just like the yeonggo. When twisted the pole with both hands to play, the fine leather straps hit the drumheads and make sounds.

Musical bow of the Kamba people of East Kenya. The string of the Uta musical bow is struck with a stick; you can either put it on the ground or on your lap. There is a similar instrument amongst the Kuria (western region), they call it Entono. 
The kamba call it "Uta wa mundu mue", which means "The bow of the medicine man"; among the swahili it is called "zera ya uta" (Zera is an Arabic word"); uta means "bow"; in the kamba community the medicin man used the bow to communicate to the spiritual world, as well as to diagnose the disease.The Kuria do not  link it to healing properties. The uta is also used in the fields, as a solo instrument; the Kamba use it  when they are going to hunt or to look for the animals to feed in the fields.
Harp-lute from the Gogo people in Tanzania, consisting of up to 14 metal strings running over an oblique bridge. The resonator is made of a calebash
Vessel rattle from Burkia Faso; resonator can be of different forms: woven basked; calebash
Bow lute (5 bows) of the Kongo-Bembe people of the Republic of Congo
Wooden sculpted flute (ca. 25 cm) with two fingerholes from the Nuni people from Burkina Faso
Single-string spike tube fiddle of the Baganda in Uganda; often decorated with a tuft of goat hair at the top of the neck

The saeng is a mouth organ with 17 bamboo pipes mounted vertically in a windchest made of dried gourd. 
Small metal boards resonate and make sounds as the musician blows in the air to the mouth piece or inhales.
Folk fiddle with a clog as resonator from Sweden
Balafo with 14 to 18 lamels arranged on a cruved base, from the Dagara people in Burkina Faso. Called Gyilli in Ghana

Five-string plucked lute of the Kongo-Bembe peoples of the Republic of the Congo. The 5 metal strings are tuned with large upright tuning pegs fitted with metal jingles. The strings are plucked with the thumb and forefinger of both hands. The instrument is used mainly to accompany singing
Fiddle (khuur) with horse head from Mongolia; two strings and trapezoid soundbox
Wooden sculpted flute (30 to 40 cm) with two fingerholes used to accompany the masked dances of the Nuni people from Burkina Faso

The pulpiri is a thick and hard leaf of tangerin or citron tree. 
It makes sound when musician blows air putting it between the lips. The strength of blowing can control the pitch.
Term used in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines for the western violin, tuned like a viola
Gulmantché term for the one-stringed spike fiddle in Burkina Faso
Compact footed barrel drum from the Mbosi people of the Plateaux region in the Republic of the Congo.
Single-string spike fiddle of Bénin
The janggu is a hourglass-shaped drum made of animal skins and wooden body. The right drum head is hit with a stick while the other head is hit with a left palm.
Played in the vertical position (hung over the shoulder on a string or leaned on the knee); players applied side string shortening (the so-called fingernail technique)

Wooden transverse flute from the Fulbe people in Burkina Fasothe Fulbe people in Burkina Faso, more specifically of the riimaaybe, 'descendants of the captives', belonging to a specific stratos of fulbe society, 'dispossessed of their cultural origins after having been captured during wars or raids, or purchased from neighbouring posers by the Fulbe... The descendants of the captives work the land in direct usufruct. The musical practices of the different social groups remain clearly differentiated. The riimaaybe musicians are more or less seasonal specialists, they only play for their own festivities, well distinct from those of the Fulbe'

The jeok is a vertical wind instrument made of bamboo, similar to the danso. 
It has five finger holes in the front and one in the back. According to the book Akhakgwebeom (Cannons of Music/Guide to the Study of the Music), one end of jeok had been carved in cross shape, but now it is just cylindrical.
Wooden griot lute from the Fulbé people of Burkina Faso
Single-string spike fiddle of the Luo people of Kenya
Cornemuse roussillonnaise
Sanza with 6 lamels from the Bissa people in Burkina Faso
Slit dtum of the Fang in Gabon

Single-stringed fiddle of the Kamba people in East Kenya, played with a long special bow, made of a special plant. Different fingering from the orutu and the ishiriri. Same function as the orutu and the ishiriri: provides the melody and may be played solo or in sets
Hautbois arménien, l'anche double est appelée 'gamish'

Small side blown horn of the Teke people in Gabon and the  Republic of the Congo. Made from an antelope horn. Serves as a means of communication and to call the spirits of the ancestors. 'Ntsiemi' means 'horn' in the Teke language

Monochord calabash half-spike lute of the Fulbe people in Burkina Faso, more specifically of the riimaaybe, 'descendants of the captives', belonging to a specific stratos of fulbe society, 'dispossessed of their cultural origins after having been captured during wars or raids, or purchased from neighbouring posers by the Fulbe... The descendants of the captives work the land in direct usufruct. The musical practices of the different social groups remain clearly differentiated. The riimaaybe musicians are more or less seasonal specialists, they only play for their own festivities, well distinct from those of the Fulbe' Sandrine Loncke, Burkina Faso. The voice of the Fulbe / La voix des Peuls, CD Le Chant du monde CNR 274 1079, 1997, CD notes, p. 25-26, 35-36

[sason, mbeka, sato] Single-string spike fiddle from Flores, Indonesia. The resonator is half a coconut shell, covered with a leaf; a flat wooden stick is inserted through the resonator and serves as a neck and peg

Indonesian fiddle from Bolaang Mongondon (North Sulawesi), on the east coast of Sulawesi, and Halmahera, Maluku. Its soundboard is half a coconut shell, usually covered with a membrane of buffalo bladder
Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) from the Nuni people in Burkina Faso

Xylophone of the Mijikenda-Giriama people of the coastal region of Kenya. The square sound box is nowadays often made of plywood. The rim of the sound box is covered in its length with sponge dempers, to avoid the contact between the sounding wooden plaques and the wooden soundbox, thus avoiding distortion of the pitch. To lower the pitch of the plaques, they are scoped inwards; to highten the pitch, the length of the bars is shortened. The kiringongo plays melodies to accompany slow  mixed dances. It is played by men.
Large side blown anthopomorphic wooden natural trumpet of the Kongo-Bembe people of Republic of the Congo
Single-string tube fiddle of Burundi with a soundbox made of cow horn

The mugo is a drum which is used to perform court festive dance "mugo." The manufacturing is same as the daego, but the drum is put on the frame and one head faces upward and hit. During the early Joseon period about 1493, eight mugo were arranged to dance "mugo." Each drum siginifies four directions and differentiated with a circle colored in four different colors, that are blue, red, white, and black
One-string spike fiddle with gourd resonator of the Moosé in Burkina Faso; noteable performer Nouss Nabil
Fiddle of the Uyghur people (mainly from the Xinjiang Uyghur autonomous region in western China); highly decorated and often with a bird (nightingale) on the pegbox

The a is one of aak musical instruments but it plays role more as a ritual object. It looks like a barrel with wide body and narrower bottom and top. The top and bottom are covered with lamb skin. The ritual assistant holds the instrument and makes sound by pounding it to the ground, and helps control the tempo of the military dancer's movement

Side drum oft he Luo people of West Kenya. The drum is made from a metal frame cut from a metal tank. It is covered by cow hide, tied together by hide ropes. The fur has been scraped in the middle of the membrane to leave a circle (both sides), to arrive at the right tone colour. Hung over the shoulder with a strap made from hide. Played with both hands or one hand and a stick. Put in the sun to tune. Used in the Ramogi "Tero buru" dance.
Lamellophone of the Iteso people of Kenya .

The dangbipa is a pear shape lute with four strings and twelve frets. It is called "gokgyeong bipa" because it has a bent neck. For Chinese music, musicians use a wooden 'bal" to pluck the strings, while they put picks in the second, third, and fourth fingers. (Gugak Center, Korea)
Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) from the Kô people in Burkina Faso
Two-stringed tube fiddle of the Han Chinese

Leg rattle of the Kikuyu people of Central Kenya. It comprises a small tin can containing stones. The upper side opening of the tin can is folded toegether.Used by the dancer to accompany traditional dances; can be combined in Kikuyu with the Njingir/Ngingir
Long elongated hourglass drum of about 130 cm from the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
Balafo with 18 lamels from the Toussian people in the west of Burkina Faso
Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) from the Winnè people in Burkina Faso
One-stringed tube fiddle of the Makonde people in south-eastern Africa (Mozambique, Tanzania)

The gyobanggo is put on a wooden frame with four legs like the jingo. However, the drum is put horizontally, so one faces upward and the other faces the floor. The body is decorated with dragon painting.
Japanese indigenous spike box fiddle, usually with three strings (but sometimes the highest string is doubled)

Calebash drum from the Yana people of Burkina Faso. Made from a round gourd of which the top is cut off and which is covered with a small goatskin membrane. It is called Binderi or Binha by the Moosè people of Burkina Faso
Short-necked bowl fiddle from South Asia; resonator is rounded and deeply waisted, the lower part is covered with skin, while the upper part is open and has the shape of an umbrella

The bow of ajaeng, according to Akhakgwebeom, is made of fine tree wood. In the present, stripped forsythia wood, which is empty inside, is used to let the sound resonate well. However, it is not sure that the fine tree described in Akhakgwebeom (1493) refers to forsythia wood.
Portugese fiddle resembling the western violin, used in Brazil during feasts
The gonghu is a plucked string instrument. The strings are tied to the resonating board one end and to the horizontal supporter the other end vertically or diagonally.

The daejaeng is a zither with fifteen strings. It has rectangular soundbox and its lower body is bent. 
The right hand plucks the strings.

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: Organo a rulli / Organetto di Barberia

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Whistle, end-blown, stopped at the end and with no fingerholes. Whistle. Often decoartedwith loose hanging strips

The gwan is one of the most important vertical wind instrument arranged in the rites, events, and banquets of royal palace. Two pipes are put together side by side and the both make sound when the musician blows the air in them. There are five finger holes to control the pitch.

1 : The tak is one of the four metal instruments that are sun, yo, and tak. 
Even though it is classified as one of the aak musical instruments, it plays role more as a ritual object. It is a kind of small bell that has nothing inside but a grip on top. The musician holds it in the left hand, and hits its body with the stick in the right hand. It is distinguished from the tak which has a tongue inside. 2 : The tak is one of the four metal instruments that are sun, yo, tak. 
Even though it is classified as one of the aak musical instruments, it plays role more as a ritual object. It is a small bell with a hand grip on top and the tongue inside the bell swings to make the bell ring.
Spike fiddle of northern Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan; resonator may be spherical like the kamanche or made from a square tin can
Hautbois de Catalogne
The sojong is a bell like metal percussion hung on a frame or on the ceiling of a shrine in temples. It makes sound when hit with  stick

The chuk consists of a square wooden box and a stand. The box has a hole in the center and a large wooden pestle called "ji" is inserted in it. Musician pounds ji and makes sound. It signals the beginning of the music, and is put in the east side of the orchestra.
Single-string spike fiddle of the Maghreb; resembles the goge

The dangjeok is a transverse wind instrument with one mouth hole and seven finger holes on top of the pipe. 
The seventh finger hole is not closed by the fingers. The term "dang" is a prefix put in the name to differentiate with indigenous instrument like daegeum, junggeum, and sogeum. The dangjeok is also called sogeum in the present because they two are the same.
Single-string fiddle of the Guaycuru people in Chaco, Argentina
The bak is made of six hard wood boards that are tied together at one end to make a fan shape when spread out. When closing the unfold wood board, it makes sound

Large single-headed barrel drum with feet carved out of the base, and which is beated with a stick. Played by the Mbosi-Makwa people  in the Republic of the Congo. Used in the Amin celebration dance and lullaby. Cf. Angoho of the Mbosi-Koyo people
A stick zither  with a resonator made of an inflated bladder. Italian traditional instrument

Shaker of the Mijkenda-Giriama and -Digo people of the coastal region of Kenya. These shakers consist of round tins which have been beaten into a square form. They are used as a set, to accompany dances. They used to be made by blacksmiths
Single-string fiddle from Albania, similar to the Gusle; in New Grove spelled as Lahutë

A polish bagpipe from Podhale region. A mouth blown instrument; four voices; has a short triple chanter-drone pipe (5+1 fingerholes) and a long drone pipe ending in a hyperbolic bell (of a clarinet type); all pipes with cylindrical bores; bag made from a goat's whole skin; formerly played solo (by shepherds, wandering musicians), nowadays in folk revival, sometimes included in Podhale bands. The ability to build and play the Podhale bagpipe, or goat, were included on the National List of Intangible Cultural Heritage
Clarinette indonésienne

The sanjo daegeum is a kind of the daegeum appropriate to play folk music. 
It has one mouth hole, a membrane hole, and six finger holes. It is shorter than the daegeum but has larger mouth hole.

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: 科曼拿（甘美兰香蕉型铜鼓）

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Rectangual raft zither made of  straw stems bound together and with the strings cut out from the stems. From  the Bwa and Samo  people in Burkina Faso

The geomungo is a six-string zither with three movable bridges and sixteen convex frets. 
It has a hollow body made of paulownia wood. Three strings are supported by the bridges while the other three are open over the frets. Musician holds a bamboo stick, called suldae, between the right index finger and long finger to plcuk and strike the string. It was one of the three string instruments of the Unified Silla Period.
Rattle made of dried fruit shells on a string. Fang people of Gabon
Fiddle from Japan, derived from the Chinese huqin
Cylindrical drum from the Toussian people in Burkina Faso
Four-string spike fiddle of Iraq; 'joza' means coconut, and refers to the coconut resonator

Drum of the Mijikenda-Giriama people of the coastal region of Kenya. The sound box is made from a long hollowed tree trunk. The membrane is made from cow  hide pinned to the trunk using pegs. The drum produces sound when struck with bare hands. It is used in the Gonda and the Mshago dance.  In most of the dances, this drum represents a man. It cannot be played alone, it is played alongside the Mabumbumbu. The musondo is an old and frequently used instrument. Some musondo have wax placed in the middle of the membrane, to arrive at the required tone colour.
Single-string fiddle of the Bukidnon people of the southern Philippines

The geum is a seven stringed zither. The body toward head side is wider while its tale side is narrow. There is no fret or bridge, but thirteen hwi which is made of mother of pearl and inlayed on the body. They mark and indicate fingering spots. With the seul, the geum was arranged for court event, rites, and banquets.
General term in the Congos (RDC and RC) for a small slit-drum carved from a wooden stick

The guridangdanso is a kind of danso. It is used to be played in Gangwon-do Province. 
It looks similar to the danso and there are five finger holes and one hole is at the back.
The bangul is a cluster of small bells, and makes sound when shaked. There are several types in different regions, and the shaman in Gyeonggi-do province uses the bangul.
Fiddle of Rajastan, India. A pear-shaped, waisted belly, completely covered with skin, gradually tapering off into a hollowed-out neck of approximately the same length as the belly
Two-stringed plucked spike lute with a loose cylindrical bridge (piece of bambou stem) from the Hausa people in Burkina Faso. It has a half-calabash soundbox
In Balinese culture, the Calung is actually a metallophonic instrument that has a one-octave range, and is generally utilized to play mid-range melodies

Shaker of the Mijikenda-Kiriama people of Coastal Kenya and the Luo people of West Kenya. The ajawa consists of a calabash covered with shells, tied in a net; the ajawa is used to accompany dances; to accompany sengenya drums and kirigongo. Used before also by the Luhya community where it is called Shimuka
Side blown horn of the Bomitaba people in the Likouala region of Republic of the Congo. Made from an antilope horn
Small wooden sculptured flute, often in the form of a stylized bird, with fingerholes, and closed at the end. From the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
Galgo chae is the set of sticks used to hit both right and left drum head of the Galgo.

Solid cylindrical (sometimes barrel or conical) drum (with or without feet carved out from the base) from the Teke-Ngangoulou people of the Plateau (Gamboma) region in the Republic of the Congo. Used to accompany songs in the ritual dances and popular festivities
The kemençe with a bottle-shaped soundboard played by Greek refugees from the Turkish Black Sea coast; also called Pontic lyra

The geongo is the largest drum among Korean percussions, and is also called "ipgo" meaning "standing drum." It is very glamourously decorated and used for music of royal event and court banquet, along with sakgo and eunggo

The sugonghu is a vertical harp with twenty one strings. 
The soundbox is in the bottom, and the frame holding the strings is trapezium. The sugonghu possessed in the National Gugak Center is the one master Ham Hwa-jin brought from Beijing in 1937. Ham as the director went to China to see and inspect the Chinese music, and bought the instrument.
Wooden flute from the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) from the Turka people in Burkina Faso

The sun is one of the four metal instruments that are tak, yo, and tak. Even though it is classified as one of the aak musical instruments, it plays role more as a ritual object. It looks like a bell put upside down with a grip made of metal strap. When civil dance performers exit and military dancers enter, the ritual assistants come together shaking the sun. Sitting next to the dancers, the sun is shaked in a regular beat

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: 喷气式管风琴 motion by gas jet

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Bambou transverse flute from the Fulbe people in Burkina Faso (made from a millet stalk), about 40 to 50 cm in length. These days, musicians prefer to have tube of forged iron, which does not go out of tune, and hardly wears out. The instrument is played obliquely so as to compensate for the absence of a prepared embouchure. the flute has 3 to 4 playing holes; the flautist can however obtain intermediate tones by fractional fingering
Slit drum from the Kongo and Bembe peoples of  the Congo's. Used to accompany the Mufueti or Masoko dance.  It is crescent shaped, played in pairs, and associated with religious and magical practices

Small fiddle of the Wielkopolska (Greater Poland), region of Poland. An instrument with medieval roots; before World War I used in Poland during the ritual part of the wedding (wedding feast) together with the wedding bagpipe (Kozioł weselny / Kozioł biały); after World War II reactivated in the S. Moniuszko Music School in Zbąszyń; now used in the folk revival, too. Almost entirely carved from one piece of wood; three strings; one of bridge's feet longer, going through an opening in the top plate and resting on the back plate, functioning as a soundpost

The sakgo is a drum hung on a wood frame decorated with phoenix and the sun on top. It was used for music of royal event and court banquet put in the west side of the orchestra. When starting the music, sakgo, eunggo, and the geongo are hit in order as a set
The tewak is actually a buoy or a tool for buoyancy that the female divers in Jeju Island use when working in the sea. It is also used for accomapying their singing.

The daegeum is a transverse wind instrument made of bamboo. 
It has a mouth hole, a membrane hole, and six finger holes on top. The extra holes, called chilseonggong, are made at the end of the instrument to balance the pitch. The daegeum is the most representative Korean traditional instrument with a long history.
The hyangpiri is a double reed wind instrument which is hold vertically. Just like the dangpiri, there are eight finger holes on the bamboo body, but the first hole is at the back.
The ojukdanso is a kind of danso which is made of black bamboo. There are five finger holes and one hole is at the back.
Mouth bow of the Fang, Gabon

The nodo, colored in red, is a set of two small drums pierced crosswise on a long pole. Each drum has two drum heads. When twisted with both hands to play, the fine leather straps hit the four drumheads and make sounds
"Two-string fiddle of western Kenya. See Siiriri" (Grove Dictionary)
Single-stringed spike fiddle from Ethiopia with a rhombus shaped resonator
Vietnamese two-string fiddle, similar to Chinese erhu
Double-headed hourglass pression drum (also known as the variable tension drum or the talking drum) from the Bwa people in Burkina Faso

The cheolhyeongeum is a metallic string instrument invented by the late master Kim Yeong-cheol in the 1940s. Kim was designated to the rope walking art holder in 1976. It is similar to not only the geomungo and the Hawaiina guitar that the musician presses and makes pitches with the round shape stick to decide and to make pitch. The cheolhyeongeum has a tool called "nongok" to make pitch and to decorate the sound. The right hand uses a pick to pluck the strings just like the suldae of geomungo. However, the musician grabs it differently as if he holds a pencil.
Sanza of the Teke, Kongo and Bembe people of the Republic of the Congo. Five to eight lamellae in metal or bamboo, mounted on a box or a board
The sanjo gayageum is used to play folk music. It also has twelve strings but has no yangidu. It is a bit smaller than the original gayageum.
Basic component of traditional folk bands in the south of the Beskid Żywiecki region, Poland
Harp-lute from the Bwa and Gouin people in Burkina Faso
Double-headed cylindrical drum from the Tamasheq people in Burkina Faso
"Metal percussion rod of the Bukusu peple of Kenya" (Grove Dictionary, 1984)
Ancient three-string fiddle of Russia and Belarussia with a pear-shaped body
The dongbal is dance prop which looks like two brazen lid. When crashing each other, it makes sound. It is similar to the bara, but much smaller

Rattle of the Mbosi people in the Plateaux region of Republic of the Congo. Two or more small dried gourds are mounted on a stick and serve as vessel rattles. Used by the griot to accompany his praise songs
Shaker of the Mijikenda people of Kenya,  made of a dried calebash. a wooden handle is put in the open neck of the calebash. Used in pairs to provide percussive sounds to the Chechemeko dance
Goblet shaped drum from the Gan people in Burkina

New Grove Dictionary, 1984: "Whithorn [May-horn]. An oboe made of gtreen willow bark twisted into a conical shape and fastened with hawthorn spines. It has a double reed made of soft willow bar pressed together. It is widely used in Europe, mainly by herdsmen for signalling; in England it was used in the Oxfordshire forests in connection with a local Whit Monday hunt. It is also sometimes played by children, itinerant vendors and tradesmen. It produces one loud sound which may be caused to fluctuate in pitch by a variation of breath pressure.
The yoryeong is a kind of metallic small bell, used in Buddhist ritual. It is structured in two parts, the bell and the grip. It makes sound when shaked like a rattle
Fiddle from Myanmar; shaped like a violin, often a highly decorated pegbox; has become obsolete now
Balafo with 14 lamels from the Lobi people in Burkina Faso

The seolsoe is a small brass bowl like percussion used in shaman ritual of Jejudo Island. 
Shamans put two seolsoe upside down on the tray and hit it with two sticks.

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: 延音钢琴（可发出持续音）

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: The sanjo ajaeng is a modified instrument with eight strings which was made in the twentieth century. It is smaller and has a straight body at the tail part different from a bit larger traditional ajaeng with a bent body at the tail. An extra resonating board is attached on the body, and the bow is made of horse hair, not the wood stick.
Pear-shaped fiddle of Bulgaria with three strings; some have sympathetic strings
Three-string fiddle of the Ilonggot people of the northern Philippines
Small wooden scultpured flute, often in the form of a stylized bird, with fingerholes, and open at the end. From the Nuni people in Burkina Faso

Dongpallang is a cup-shaped metal bell part at the end of wooden body of the taepyeongso. 
The name was originated from its material, the copper, but nowadays, it is made of alloy to prevent it becoming rusty.

The hwa is a mouth organ with 13 bamboo pipes mounted vertically in a windchest made of dried gourd. 
Small metal boards resonate and make sounds as the musician blows in the air to the mouth piece or inhales.
Xylophone of the Fang of Gabon

Goblet-shaped drum of the Luhya-Isukha people of West Kenya. The sound box is  a log carved out, leaving out two protuberances to put the strap through. A lizzard skin is attached to the log with pins going through a rubber strap to hold the skin. Isikuti are played in sets of three; this is the smallest one, representing the child of the family. The drum is tuned by placing it next to the fire. The isikuti omwana keeps the constant rhythm; plays the highest tone; is played with the palms of the hands, while hung around the shoulder. It accompanies the isikuti dances and is used for communcaiton, as a signal instrument; the people know what the rhythm means: 'something is happening, let's go and see

Kettle drum from the Yana people in Burkina Faso. Made of a calebash of which the top has been cut off and covered with a membrane. To be compared with the Bendré, but the skin glued to the calebash covers a bigger part of the resonator. Unlike the Bendré there are no cords to stretch the skin
Double-headed cylindrical drum from the Gulmancé people in Burkina Faso
Gaktoe is a wood stick with cow horn attached at one end.  It is used to hit and to make sound of pyeonjong, pyeongyeong, teukjong, teukgyeong, and banghyang

Idioglot transverse clarinet of the Bissa people in Burkina Faso. Made from a hollowed-out millet stalk. It has two small gourd resonators with side windows placed over the ends of the stalk. It usually has a finger-hole at the distal end which may be stopped by the left thumb. http://inconstantsol.blogspot.be/2014/01/musique-bisa-de-haute-volta-rec-1961.html

Longitudinal wooden drum from the Kongo and Vili people of the Kouilou region (Pointe-Noire) in the Republic of the Congo. Played horizontally, with a handle carved in the wooden sound box. Used for the healing ritual called ' n'assi ', for popular festivities and also used for communication
Cylindro-concial drum of the Konda and Yembe peoples of the DRC. The name is also used for the footed conical drum of the Kongo and Bembe peoples of the Republic of Congo
The jeolgo is a drum which is slantly put on a square support. One side of the drum fits in the space carved.  Musician hits the drum head which faces upward

A type of drum played with both bare hands. It is in widespread use primarily in Mali and Guinea among the Maninka and Susu peoples, and also in neighbouring Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso; it is also perhaps the most popular African drum outside the African continent
A common term (with many variants) used generically for many kinds of drum among the numerous Bantu-speaking peoples of central, eastern-central and southern Africa
(i) Short-necked fiddle from Turkey with a bottle-shaped soundboard and three strings; (ii) in Western Turkey the kemençe is similar to the Greek lyra with a pear shaped soundboard and three strings
Generic term for Chinese fiddle, literally 'barbarian string instrument'
Balafon, played in ensemble (solo, bass, accompaniments) of the Nzime people in the Sangha region, close to the Cameroun border
Rectangular 'raft' rattle from the Mijikenda people in Kenya, consisting of a tray-shaped box made from made of straw stems bound together, with seeds inside

The galgo is almost the same as the janggu in its size and shape, but the musician uses two sticks in both hands. The direction for tightening the drum heads are different that it can tighten both sides while the Janggu can only tighten toward the right side
A musical tool used to make the so-called musical racket; nowadays used as percussion instrument in folk bands in Kaszuby (Cassubia) Poland, and is a symbol of the region's musical identity

Traditional Andean, lowland and Central American single-skin frame drum with handle. The mestizo bombo, e.g. the Argentinean and Chilean bombo is a double-skin cylindrical drum. The Argentinean 'bombo legüero' is a barrel drum
Single-string spike fiddle of the Baggara people of Sudan
Turkish fiddle, originally a gourd spike-fiddle (type of kabak = 'gourd fiddle')

A seasonal, polish folk instrument, made in the spring; would become porous and unplayable when it dried out; formerly a signal instrument (used by shepherds), often played by children, nowadays sometimes made as a music toy; body made from a spirally rolled piece of willow bark, fastened with a thorn ('przetyczka'); it should have a double reed ('bekas'), also made of willow bark, in the inlet

The sogeum is a transverse wind instrument made of bamboo shorter than the daegeum. 
Along with the daegeum and junggeum, it is one of the three bamboo flutes of the Unified Silla Period. According to Akhakgwebeom it is said to be the same as the structure of daegeum, but the sogeum has no membrane hole and shorter than the junggeum. It only has one mouth hole and six finger holes. No written record about it had been found since described in Akhakgwebeom, and the sogeum is considered to be the same as the dangjeok of the present time, and both names are used to refer one same instrument.
Barrel drum of the Banda-Ngbugu in Central African Republic

Rattle of the Kongo -Bembe and Kongo-Minkengue people in the Bouenza  region of Republic of the Congo. Two or more small dried gourds are mounted on a stick and serve as vessel rattles. Used by the griot to accompany his praise songs
Apache fiddle made from a hollowed-out agave stalk, with two or three strings; often decorated with geometrical or natural designs; also called tsi edo atl
Portable eight plaque bass xylophone from the Bomitaba  people of the Likouala region in the north of the Republic of the Congo
Two-stringed spike fiddle from China, with a resonator made from gourd; the pegbox of the one from MIM Phoenix has a 'fantasy' wooden design
A North African term for an oblique rim-blown flute

Idioglot transverse clarinet from the Nuni people in Burkina Faso. Made from a hollowed-out millet stalk. To be compared with the Bumpan of the Bissa people in Burkina Faso, but without the  small gourd resonators over the ends of the stalk
Single-string fiddle from Latvia, with a bladder resonator; it is played vertically
The bow of haegeum is made of bamboo and the hair of horse tail. It is inserted in between the two strings.

The dok is one of aak musical instruments but it plays role more as a ritual object. It is a long cylindrical box without a bottom and painted in redish black color. There are two holes at each side of the top. The player holds the cylinder both hand and pounds it to the ground to control the dance movement.

Hyeo is the double-reed inserted into the bamboo pipe of the Piri or Taepyeongso. 
The musicians hold and blow the air into the seo to shake and resonate the pipe. Piri Hyeo is made by planing the bamboo bark and Taepyeongso Hyeo is made of reed
Single-string tube fiddle of the Hima in Rwanda and northeastern DR Congo
Single-string half spike fiddle from the Daza and Teda of Tibesti and Ouaddai in Chad
[kora, sasong, rebang] Single-string spike fiddle of Flores in Indonesia; the resonator is half a coconut shell, covered with a sago palm-leaf sheath
Suldae is the stick-like pick used to pluck the strings of geomungo and hyangbipa. Musicians hold and grab it in their right hand. It is also called "sul" or "si"

Jin is the bamboo stick used to hit and to scrape the eo. 
The stick is made of three bamboo pieces each of which are again split into three piece at one end and thus nine pieces
Elongated hourglass drum from the Winnè people in Burkina Faso
The doldanso is a kind of danso which is made of stone. There are five finger holes and one hole is at the back.
Two-stringed fiddle of the Karakalpak, Kazakh and Kirghiz people of Central Asia; resonator is a deeply carved out ladle, the bottom half is covered with skin

"Single-headed conical drum of the Digo people of Kenya. The membrane is fixed by a thick securing ring and a small number of cords. The drum may be used as part of a tuned set with the mchirima" (Grove Dictionary)
Plain cylindrical footed drum from the Mbosi-Koyo people of the Cuvette region (Owando) in the Republic of Congo. Used in a dance to celebrate the birth of twins called 'Okera'

The eo is wooden tiger-shaped percussion, played by a bamboo stick hitting the head three times and scraping the sawlike top once. This signals the end of the music. It is colored in white and put in the west side of the orchestra.
Flûte oblique égyptienne en bambou à 3 sections et 6 trous de jeu
'Ox leg' two-stringed fiddle of the Dong people in Guizhou, south-western China (shape is that of an ox leg, hence the name)
Elongated hourglass drum from the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
Three-string spike fiddle from Cambodja, resembles the Javanese rebab
Animal horn with mouthpiece cut out on the outer curved side of the horn, with an additional whole which serves as a fingerhole. From the Nuni people in Burkina Faso
Flûte oblique de Sumatra

New Grove dictionary, 1984: "Buzzer [spinning disc]. A free aerophone, akin to the bullroarer but distinguished from it in that a buzzer (usually shpaed like a disc, less often a blade) has two holes through which a cord is threaded and the ends tied together. The player holds the cord and swings it rapidly to twist it; an outward pull on the cord causes it to unwind rapidly and then wind up again in the opposite direction, the disc meanwhile making a humming sound. Buzzers are known as toys but are also often associated with ritual or magic. Examples include 'fir-fur', 'koororohuu', 'ukas', 'umampembe' and 'uvuru'. 
New Grove dictionary, 1984: "Whirling aerophone. Term used in the Hornbostel-Sachs classification (412.22), exemplified by the 'bullroarer' and the 'whirring disc' (see 'buzzer')"

Norwegian folk fiddle, resembling the violin, with 4 melody strings and 4 sympathetic strings; often elaborately decorated with geometrical and vegetal designs, with the head of a Norwegian lion or dragon on the pegbox
Side blown horn of the Teke people in the Plateaux region of Republic of the Congo. Made from an antelope horn. Protects against lightning and serves as a means of communication
Goblet drum from the Mbosi ans Makwa people of the Cuvette region (Makoua) in the Republic of the Congo. Used in the Ondzambé dance
Mongolian two-stringed spike tube fiddle, mostly used in ensembles
Two-string spike fiddle from Cambodja, resembles the Thai so u with a resonator of coconut
Wooden flute from the Nuni people in Burkina Faso

Dolgwea is peg used for the string instruments, such as gayageum and geomungo, to hold the strings and to connect them to the back of the instrument body. 
It is also used to tighten the strings. Musicians can tune the pitch very accurately by turning it to tighten and to release the strings.

A kind of trumpet (straight labrosone) with a conical profile, made from a trunk of a young tree that is cut along in two halves, then each is hollowed, and finally both are put back together with the help of pitch; formerly used for apotropaic purposes (while making the ritual uproar) and signalling (shepherds, fishermen, firefighters, to signal the beginning of rituals and ceremonies); nowadays as part of folk revival; a symbol of Cassubians' ethnic identity (Kaszuby, the region of Poland)

The eung is one of aak musical instruments but it plays role more as a ritual object. When the civil dance performers exit and the military dancers enter, one music assistant bring it. Standing next to the dancers, the assistant plays it following the beat of the Jingo. The eung looks similar to the chuk, but has longer and narrower body. The assistant pounds the eung once with the pestle and then hits the right and left side.

The moktak is a wood block used in Buddhist ritual. 
The inside of wood block is empty so the sound resonates well when hit with a wood stick.
The muljanggu, literally water drum, is a percussion that is a gourd bowl which is put face down in a big pot filled half with water

The togo is a drum with clay body and clay stick, called "goebu." The animal skin is covered on both side of the barrel-like body. It had been used during the early Joseon Dynasty, but it seems not to be used any more
Hautbois droit ou courbe du Népal
Harp-lute from Burkina Faso. Seven or eight strings. The resonator is a half or three quarter calebash
Transverse flute from the Gulmancé people in the est of Burkina Faso. Tube in bambou or plastic; often covered with leather. Four fingerholes
Fiddle from Armenia, with rectangular soundboard and 3 or 4 strings
Compact cylindrical footed drum from the Teke-Kukuya people in the Republic of Congo. Used to accompany the song during the ritual dances and popular festivities

Dance rattle of the Pokomo people of the coastal region of Kenya. To make the Msewe, small vessel rattles are made in a large number and painted in red, blue, green, natural, and then sewn on a chord. When they are made, they are still green, the maker dries them in the sun before putting on the chord. They are wound around the leg three times, like a snake. The length of the rattle depends on the size of the leg.
Rattle made of dried fruit shells attached to a leather stick, used in Gabn
Vessel rattle of the Teke-Ngangoulou people of the Plateaux region in Republic of the Congo. Made of a small calebash, filled with grains of which the neck is closed with a cork
The teukjong is a single large size bronze bell hung on the wooden frame, and makes sounds when hit by the cow horn stick. It was arranged in court ceremonial music

The abak is dance prop which is made of six boards made of ivory or bone of whale, cow or deer. It is smaller than the bak. It makes sound when a musician unfolds the boards making fan shape, and closes them
Okjeok is a transverse wind instrument made of jade. Like the daegeum, it has one mouth hole, a membrane hole, and six finger holes.

Pedal accordion, bellows connected to the instrument with a two-piece pipe. After World War I the accordion became a popular component of polish folk bands (together with the violin and the drum); the pedal type being especially popular in Mazovia on the right side of the Vistula river (the region of Kurpie and the area of Garwolin), to some degree also in Podlasie (Podlachia)
The mulheobeok is a water jar which can be also used to beat a rhythm for singing. The left hand hits the rim of the mouth while the right hand hits its shoulder with a stick. (Gugak Center, Korea)
Single-string spike fiddle with gourd resonator from Western Africa, term used by Hausa and Yoruba people in ia Nigeria and Niger
Argyle ocarina from the Yana people in Burkina Faso

A kind of horn (conical profile), made from a branch that is cut along in two halves, then each is hollowed, and finally both are put back together with the help of pitch and metal hoops; formerly used as a signal instrument (mainly in herding); since 19th c. used during Advent and watchnight service on Christmas Eve (mainly in north-east and east regions of Poland); nowadays as part of folk revival

Conical or cylindrical drum of the Teke people of the Plateaux region in Republic of the Congo, made from the holow trunk of a tree, on to one opening of which is nailed an antelope skin. The nails are covered by a strip made from caoutchouc

The nogo is a set of two drums pierced crosswise by a pole and hung in a wooden frame. 
Each drum colored in red has two drum heads so it has four drum heads. It is arranged in sacrificial rites for human spirits

Metal rattle of the Luo people of West Kenya, made of a metal wire attached to a wooden  handle. On the wire metal bottle tops are inserted through a whole in their middle on the metal round wire. The bottle tops have been flattened and then held in the fire; which softens the tone. The rattle is used to accompany and enrich the rhythmic texture.The shaker is played by women, played for instance in Dodo dance (female dance).
Talking drum (double-headed hourglass drum; variable tension drum) from the Bobo people in Burkina Faso
[gonje] Single-string spike fiddle of the Dagbamba people of Ghana

Spike fiddle from Rajasthan and Gujarat, north-west India; the resonator consists of half a coconut shell; there are simple forms with only two strings, and more complex ones which have sympathetic strings as well and are decorated with tassles and fabric, the bow may be decorated with bells
Hautbois cylindrique à anche double idioglotte, présent en Chine
Rattle made of a rectangular flat dried fruit, used by the Teke-Ngangoulou people of the Plateaux region in Republic of the Congo to accompany their dances
The daegonghu is a harp-like instrument with twenty three strings bigger than sogonghu. It has a bent neck and musician uses both hands to play it holding it around his waist.
Small double-headed cylindrical drum from the Nuni people of Burkina Faso
The  consists of sixteen bronze bells all in different pitch hung on a wooden frame, and is played with a stick made of cow horn. It was arranged in court ceremonial music
The hyangbal is dance prop for hyangbal dance. It looks like brazen lid. When crashing each other, it makes sound. It is similar to the dongbal, but much smaller

Cylindrical drum of the Luo people of West Kenya. The ohangla is a big metal container covered on both sides with cow hide, linked together by cow hide stripes. Strap to carry it around. They are used in the Ohangla dance, played in a set of six, with two sticks. They are tuned to different pitches and played by men.

The nzumari oboe is an adaptation of the Arab zurna and zummara, introduced when the Arabs came to trade on the Coastal regions of Kenya. The nzumari is a solo instrument, used in dancing ceremonies during the interludes. It accompanies the singing (in unisono) and is played in between the verses of the songs, which tell  the occasion (wedding, funeral, harvest, child birth). They sing the song and people respond to it: call and respons. The nzumari player uses the circular breathing (the cheeks have to be blown up) to attain a continuous sound. The nzumari is played only by men and only for special occasions like weddings

Wooden double bell of the Kongo-Vili people in the Kouilou region near the Atlantic coast in the Republic of the Congo. Geometrical decoration engraved and burned. Used by the Nganga, healer and spiritualist, the hourglass shaped double bell is liked to Nkisi cult worship and is used during songs and dances to treat the ill. It is also played during twin birth ceremonies
Vessel rattle made from a big dried longitudinal bean-like fruit, from the Teke people in the Plateaux region of Republic of the Congo
Wooden goblet drum from the Samogo people in Burkina Faso
Wooden lute from the Moosè people in Burkina Faso
Single-headed open frame drums of the Yoruba people of Nigeria and Benin. It has an earthenware frame and either sticks or bamboo pegs for adjusting tension
[sekhankula] Single-string fiddle from southern Africa, mainly among Sotho people; it has a tin can resonator

The sajanggu is a kind of hourglass drum of which is made of two clay pot lids. A wooden hoop is inserted between the lids so that it is shaped to be an hourglass drum. The performing technique is same as the janggu, and no stick is used for the left hand
Two-string fiddle of the Han Chinese; resonator is coconut or gourd, covered with wooden soundboard; it has laterally inserted tuning pegs
Wooden whistle open at the end and with fingerholes. From the Kô people in Burkina Faso
Chad ensemble of calebashes, the biggest one used as recipient filled with water in which the two smaller ones are beaten
Harp-lute from the Turka people from Burkina Faso. Often with a metal buzzer at the end of the neck

The danso is a vertical wind instrument made of bamboo. It looks similar to the tungso but much thinner and shorter. 
There are five finger holes and one is in the back.
Scraped slit stick of the Kongo, Bembe and Suku peoples of the Congo's. It is a hollowed stick or bamboo tube with a lengthwise slit
Panflute of the Kikuyu people of Central Kenya.

The u is a mouth organ with 36 bamboo pipes mounted vertically in a windchest made of dried gourd. 
Small metal boards resonate and make sounds as the musician blows in the air to the mouth piece or inhales.
Spike fiddle (of the Toraja) in Sulawesi Selatan (South Sulawesi)
Spike fiddle from northern Sumatra from the Batak people
Polish folk double bass; size not standarized
Kettle drum from the Tamasheq people in the Northern Gorom Gorom department of Burkina Faso
Two-string fiddle of the Han Chinese; resonator is coconut, covered with wooden soundboard; bridge is usually a sea-shell; resembles banhu but pegs are dorsally inserted
General term for single string fiddle played in central India by tribal groups

Hindustani classical sarangi: short-necked fiddle, soundbox is made from one piece of wood, covered with skin; membrane is waisted; it has three playing strings and (many) sympathetic strings. Nepali sarangi: small short-necked fiddle made from one piece of wood; the lower part of the soundbox is covered with skin, the upper part is open; it typically has 4 strings; not to be confused with sarinda (see below)
Hautbois du Couserans, France

The sogonghu is the smallest harp-like instrument with thirteen strings. It has a bent soundbox and horizontal supporter to hold strings vertically. The sogonghu possessed in the National Gugak Center is the one master Ham Hwa-jin brought from Beijing in 1937. Ham as the director went to China to see and inspect the Chinese music, and bought the instrument.
idiophonic voice disguiser
