The jeolgeum is the foldable gayageum. At the back of its body, there is a line, which looks like a crack, and screws to open and to fold the instrument.

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#altL.@value: Violí amb trompa, Violí amb botzina

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: A term for various chordophones, both fiddles and lutes; within the Formalized Fiddle it may refer to the Javanese rabab, the Arabic box spike fiddle, and the north African rabab
A term which in its many linguistic variant forms denotes a number of types of lamellophones found mainly in the Congo's and bordering countries
Hautbois du Bigorre, France
Side-blown flute from the Peul people in Senegal. Named after the cane's name out of which it is made. Mouthpiece made of wax. Often covered in colourful textile
Anthropomorphic fiddle of the Holo and Suku people of southwestern DR Congo and northern Angola; the head is the pegbox; the soundboard is a thin wooden board

A ritual music tool; made of a handle (wrapped with string) with three branches, each with a clapper bell; an attribute of ritual wedding figures (marshal, best men); used in the Lubelskie province, Poland; it was shaken to produce ringing to accompany singing
Balafo with 14 lamels from the Pougouly people in Burkina Faso

Percussion instruments of the Mijikenda people of the coastal region of Kenya.  A silver-coloured plate is put on a wooden round feeted stand. The plate is held in place by a nail. The stand has three feet, nailed on the wooden plate. It is played by a wooden stick without rubber. The upatsu is a loud percussion instrument and is used to accompany mabumbumbu and the musondo drums, in the Mshago dance. It is also played with nzumari and bungo.
Vessel rattle of the Mobsi-Koyo people of Republic of the Congo. Made of a small calebash, of which the neck is closed with a cork

A bagpipe with 16th c. roots; the biggest of Polish bagpipes with the lowest tuning and an elegiac sound; traditional element of folk bands in west Greater Poland (along with violins and, after World War I, an E-flat clarinet)

Guimbarde originaire du Cambodge. Il en existe deux sortes : la première, en métal, possède une languette hétéroglotte alourdie à son extrémité par une boule de cire. La deuxième, fabriquée en bambou, a une languette idioglotte
Balafo with 15 lamels from the Turka people in Burkina Faso
Idiophone drum from the Fulsé people in the Pobé Mengao department of Burkina Faso. Made from a gourd cut in two and carved out

Large oboe of the Mijikenda-Giriama people of the coastal region of Kenya. . The bung'o oboe consists of three parts: a cylindrical bamboo tube with 3 fingerholes for pitch variation, a conical bell in wood; and double reed with pirouette. 
The large oboe is a solo instrument, used in the Sengenya dance, played during the short intervals and signalling the movement of the dances. The songs will tell the occasion (wedding, funeral, harvest, child birth). They sing the song and people respond to it: call and respons
Single-string fiddle of the Berbers of southern Morocco, with a round soundbox covered with skin; the peg is inserted laterally and the string runs in an angle over the soundboard
Bowl lyre of the Luo people from Kenya
Single-string spike fiddle of the Touareg in northern Africa, with a calabash resonator and often two soundholes in the membrane
Bell hung on sheep's neck as a signalization (formerly also for apotropaic purposes)
Generic term for several instruments in Madagascar; here it refers to fiddles from Madagascar
Two-string fiddle of Laos, with a jackwood or bamboo soundbox

The sepiri is a double reed instrument similar to the hyangpiri with the eight finger holes and the first hole at the back. 
Its volume is weaker than hyangpiri and used for small ensemble with string instruments.

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#pref.@value: 舌头放在唇间发出的声音？

The sogwanja is a vertical wind instrument used by shepard boy in the past. 
It was made of bone of large bird or old yellow bamboo. There are one mouth hole and three finger holes all in one side.
Europese volksvedel met een blaas als resonator
Hautbois des Balkans

The seul is a zither with twenty five strings. It is colorfully decorated with clouds and cranes, and the strings are dyed in orange. Left hand plucks the strings above the thirteenth string, which is not used, and the right hand plucks the strings below the thirteenth string. Each set of twelve strings is in an octave difference.
Keyed fiddle from Scandinavia and northern Germany, with melody strings, bourdon strings and sympathetic strings; it plays an important role in Swedish folk music

The pyeongjodanso is a kind of danso. It has a thicker body and the tones are perfect fourth lower than the tones sound from the danso. 
There are five finger holes and one is at the back.
Single-string fiddle of the southern Philippines

The Dojagi janggu (celadon hourglass drum) was discovered in the historical site of the Goryeo Dynasty. It has thinner round tube, so the waist is slimmer and longer compared to the janggu used in the present, and the shape and size of the body are different

The Jabara is two thin brass plates which looks like a round lid, and the cloth hand grip are tied through the holes pieced at the bulging part, that is at the center of each plate. 
It makes sound when two plates are clashed. It is larger than the dongbal and hyangbal which are used in the dance.
Pair of goblet drum from the Sahel people in Burkina Faso, near the border with Mali
Single-string spike fiddle from Manipur, north-eastern India without tuning peg (string is directly attached to the neck); it comes with a large iron bow with bells on it
Three-stringed fiddle of the Lunda and Chokwe people of southern DR Congo, northeastern Angola and northern Zambia

Two-stringed fiddle of the Kikuyu people of Central Kenya. The soundbox is covered on both sides. Two metal string pegs (used to be made of wood), placed parallel to the soundbox. Movable bridge. The membrane is nailed on the soundbox with metal nails. Both the mbeve and the orutu / ishiriri bow can be used. The kikuyu also use the long bow under the influence of the Kamba community. The wandindi has the same function as the other fiddles.
Tamasheq term for the griot lute in Burkina Faso
Stick zither with a notched bridge, which supports its five strings in a plane at right angles to that of the string-bearer. Unique to the area of western central Africa
The bu is a clay pot placed on the wooden frame and beaten with a bamboo whisk which is splited at one end. Musician hits the rim of the instrument
Long fiddle from Lithuania, with a bladder as resonator, over which run the strings; it is played vertically, standing on the ground
Four-string fiddle of the Han Chinese (si = four)
Musical bow of the Bissa people of Burkina Faso. It has a metal string and a resonator made of a calabash cut in two. The top part of the calabas may be attached to the upper part of the bow
Goblet drum of the Kota people in Gabon
Tuvan four-stringed spike tube fiddle
Three-stringed fiddle from the Wends or Sorbs of eastern Germany and Slavonic countries; soundboard is waisted, the instrument looks like a primitive violin

The soribuk looks same as the yonggo in its shape and size except for the dragon painting. Instead of using ropes to pull and to strech skin of the both drum heads, metal tacks fix the skin on the body. Different from the yonggo, the drum is put on the floor and the heads face left and right. The drummer most of the time uses it to accompany pansori and always plays it sitting on the floor.

The hyangbipa is a lute with five strings. It has straight neck with ten frets. It is played with the suldae to pluck and to strike the strings, but nowadays musicians use fingers as well. It is one of the three indigenous string instruments of the Unified Silla Period.
Short-necked fiddle with large round soundboard from Rajasthan, played by the Manghaniyar caste
One- or two-stringed spike fiddle of the Dayak in Borneo

A portable xylophone of the Sara, Barma and neighbouring peoples of southern Chad. The keys are strung together each above a gourd resonator, which can be either curved or staight and is fitted with a mirliton made of a fish bladder, bat's wing or spider's web

Large lyre, created by Dominic Ogari, as a base version of the Obokano. The sound box is a carved out log. Twelve nylon strings, in yellow, red, blue and green. Five small sticks glued horizontally together form the bridge. The rikano is three obokano in one. Three different tunings are possible, to play three different kinds of repertory. When the player is not singing, he can change the tunings during the performance. Played during dance performance, single or when ientertaining people. There are only two versions up til now : one in California (Los Angeles), one in Nairobi. "Ri" is the Abagusii word for Giant.
The teukgyeong is a stone hung on the wooden frame and makes sounds when hit by the cow horn stick. It was arranged in court ceremonial music.

The gayageum is twelve-string zither which makes sounds when the strings are plucked and strummed. On the rectangular soundboard made of paulownia wood, twelve movable bridges support the twisted silk strings. It is one of the three string instruments of the Unified Silla Period.
Two-string fiddle of Thailand, with a coconut resonator with a carved out back and skin soundtable
The pyeongyeong is consisted of sixteen stones all in different pitch hung on a wooden frame, and is played with a stick made of cow horn. It was arranged in court ceremonial music.
The pungmulbuk is a barrel drum. The skin of two drum heads are connected with the rope in a round body. Musician uses a stick made of birch to strike the drum head
Two-stringed tube fiddle from Guangdong or Fujian, with wooden tubular resonator and wooden soundboard
